claims.text: AlCrFeNiSi feedstock particles will be engineered with a thin shell enriched in Ni and Si.
Enrichment of the shell in Ni and Si will lower its melting point relative to the AlCrFeNiSi core.
During laser processing, the modified shell will melt before the particle core.
Early shell melting will form a transient liquid phase at the particle surface.
The transient liquid phase will create localized liquid bridges between particles.
The core–shell feedstock will produce a graded microstructure.
Early shell melting will disperse and moderate thermal influx during laser exposure.
The transient liquid phase will smooth temperature gradients during solidification.
The transient liquid phase will enhance interparticle bonding and promote more uniform solidification.
Smoother thermal gradients and transient-liquid-assisted bonding will enable local thermal-stress relaxation.
Core–shell AlCrFeNiSi powder will reduce residual thermal stresses relative to homogeneous AlCrFeNiSi powder processed under identical conditions.
Core–shell AlCrFeNiSi powder will reduce processing-induced microcracking and other defects.
Components made from the core–shell powder will have higher yield strength than components made from homogeneous powder.
Components made from the core–shell powder will have greater ductility than components made from homogeneous powder.
The intervention is intended for miniature components with typical dimensions below 10 mm.
The proposed processing window uses substrate preheating below 200 °C.
The process must melt the modified shell while leaving the particle core mostly solid.
The intervention's benefits may be lost when laser power or scanning speed does not permit controlled shell melting.
Rapid heat dissipation is particularly critical for sub-10 mm components.
Homogeneous AlCrFeNiSi powder processed under high thermal gradients leads to residual stress and degraded mechanical properties.
